new_statements.quote: The diphthongs are the same as Baki with oi added. It is differently accented from the Baki. Though the accent most frequently falls on the penultimate, many words of three syllables are accented on the first, and a number of four-syllabled words are accented on the first and third.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (archive.org southsealanguage02macduoft, full view). The PDF text at pp. 130-131 (printed pp. 98-99) and the saved 100-dpi page scan both carry the quoted passage word for word: 'The diphthongs are the same as Baki with oi added. It is differently accented from the Baki. Though the accent most frequently falls on the penultimate, many words of three syllables are accented on the first, and a number of four-syllabled words are accented on the first and third.' (image italicises 'first', 'first', 'third'). It sits in Fraser's introductory remarks on sounds, immediately before 'THE ARTICLE', exactly as the locator says. I also confirmed the secondary remark at printed pp. 104-105…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word accent on the penultimate syllable, but with a sizeable class of exceptions: many trisyllabic words carry accent on the initial syllable (i.e. antepenult), and some four-syllable words are accented on the first and third syllables (initial + penult). Fraser contrasts this with Baki, which he describes (same volume p. 74) as regularly penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only implicit: four-syllable words 'accented on the first and third' (two prominences; which is primary is not said).
new_statements.exceptions: Many trisyllables accented on the first syllable; some quadrisyllables on first and third. Separately (pp. 104-105) verbs beginning in ma/me/mi/mo/mu 'and accented on the first syllable' do not take the realis m- prefix. Also notes frequent dropping of final syllables (nikambo > nikam, nagku > nag), which bears on where the penult is counted.
new_statements.domain_note: Impressionistic missionary description of word accent in citation forms; no phonetic correlates, no examples with accent marks, no phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Fraser 1891 calls the language 'Bierian' (Ray 1893 'Bieri', corrected to Bieria in Ray 1926:229 per Lynch & Crowley 2001:105); it is the language of Vovo village, south Epi = Tryon 1976 list 142 'Vowa (Epi)' = Glottolog bier1246 / ISO brj. Not to be confused with Tryon's list 104/105 'Vovo', a Malakula language (Lynch & Crowley 2001 sec. 3.7.20). Fraser's description is of 1890s missionary-era Bieria; the language had ~25 speakers in 1999 and is shifting to Nakanamanga.
